title: The Unix Parallel — Small Tools Piped Together, 55 Years Later

panels.text: In 1964, Doug McIlroy — head of the Computing Techniques Research Department at Bell Labs — wrote an internal memo. He wanted a way to connect programs together "like a garden hose — screw in another segment when it becomes necessary to massage data in another way."

panels.prompt: McIlroy's garden hose metaphor illustrated: literal garden hose segments being screwed together in a row, each segment labeled with a different capability — filter, sort, count, transform — with water (representing data) flowing through them from left to right, lush green garden setting, whimsical and educational. Below the hoses, the same visual repeated but with glowing AI agent icons instead of hose segments, and glowing file documents instead of water flowing between them. Comic book style, warm editorial illustration with ink lines and watercolor washes, emerald green accent

panels.text: His vision became the Unix pipe: the | character that chains small programs together. cat file | grep pattern | sort | uniq. Four small tools. None knows about the others. Each reads text in and writes text out. Complex behavior emerges from simple, composable parts.

panels.caption: The same fundamental design pattern, rediscovered across half a century

panels.text: In 1978, McIlroy articulated the philosophy: "Write programs that do one thing and do it well. Write programs to work together. Write programs to handle text streams, because that is a universal interface."

This is not merely an analogy. Both Unix pipes and multi-agent file communication solve the same fundamental design problem: how do you build complex behavior from simple, composable, interchangeable parts? Both reject the monolithic approach in favor of modular composition. Both use text as the universal interface.

panels.speaker: ZENBOT

panels.text: "The best ideas in computing are not inventions — they are principles. Composition through text has been rediscovered over half a century, at new scales, solving new problems. It is an immortal idea."

McIlroy was thinking about text processing in 1964. He could not have imagined AI agents in 2025. But the principle — compose small, focused tools through universal interfaces — transcends the technology. Fifty-five years. The longest-running good idea in computing.

panels.text: Multi-agent systems are the newest layer in a stack that is 90 years tall — from Turing's imaginary tape machine to swarms of coordinating AI agents. And there is one more secret hiding in this issue. It involves YOU, right now, reading these words.
